title_en: Why Xi'an Is No Place for the Young: Three Cases Say It All
excerpt_en: A rocket engineer's official letter, a subway line's substandard cables, and a mining contract fought over for fourteen years — three famous cases, one operating system: rank and connections outrank rules and contracts, and the young pay the price.
body_en:
An official letter about a rocket engineer, the cables of Metro Line 3, and a hundred-billion-yuan mining contract fought over for fourteen years — three nationally famous cases, all telling the same story.

You don't need a tourism video to judge whether a city suits young people. Look at three things: how it prices talent, how it enforces its own rules, and whether it honors the contracts it signs.

In Xi'an, unfortunately, each of the three has a famous case study.

Zhang Xiaoping: a man's price is set by his rank

In September 2018, an official document bearing a red seal went viral and pushed the Xi'an Aerospace Propulsion Institute onto front pages across China.

Zhang Xiaoping joined the institute in 1994 and spent 24 years building rocket engines, rising to deputy chief designer for cryogenic propellant engines — a researcher-grade post — working on programs including the 480-ton-thrust liquid-oxygen/kerosene engine meant for future crewed lunar missions. In March 2018 he resigned and joined LandSpace, a private rocket company in Beijing. According to the article that detonated the story, his salary at the institute had been 120,000 yuan a year; his new employer was said to be paying close to a million.

The institute panicked. But it did not reach for the market's tools — no raise, no counter-offer. Instead it filed a document with the Xi'an labor arbitration commission, titled “Account of Zhang Xiaoping's Participation in Our Institute's Programs.” In that document, Zhang was suddenly irreplaceable: his departure, it said, “could to some extent affect the progress of China's crewed lunar landing program.”

Sit with the absurdity for a moment. While he was there, he was a mid-level technical cadre on a salary of a little over a hundred thousand yuan, waiting his turn in a narrow promotion queue — dispensable. The moment he walked out, the paperwork made him priceless, a man whose exit could sway a moon program. Same person, two prices; the only difference was which story the organization needed that day. Afterwards, Liu Zhirang, president of the Academy of Aerospace Propulsion Technology, publicly admitted the document had exaggerated for the sake of the arbitration, and the institute conceded what everyone knew: promotion channels are narrow, pay is low, and talent keeps leaving.

That admission is the most honest part of the whole affair. Whether Zhang was worth 120,000 or a million, the market had long given its answer; the institute — and the system it represents — had neither the authority nor the mechanism to accept it. Inside that system, a person's price is set by rank, not by contribution; by the organization, not by the market. Want to leave? Fine — after the secrecy cooling-off period, after arbitration, after the organizational procedures. When people cannot be kept, power is used to hold them in place.

A young engineer reading this case can do his own math: however good you are, inside this system your ceiling is your rank. The only exception is to leave first — only after you leave do you suddenly become important.

The Metro cables: a subway line's safety, saved by a laid-off employee's post

On March 13, 2017, a post appeared online: “Do You Still Dare to Ride the Xi'an Metro?” The author said he was a former employee of Shaanxi Aokai Cable Co., and that the cables used in Xi'an Metro Line 3 were fakes — 70-square-millimeter wire dressed up as 95.

He was right. A State Council circular (Guobanfa [2017] No. 56) later confirmed that from August 2014 to the end of 2016, Line 3 had been built with Aokai's substandard cables in its lighting and air-conditioning circuits — a buried safety hazard. How did the company win the contract? Exactly as the circular put it: low-price bidding, plus bribes to staff at the metro company and the construction firms. And the regulators? The Xi'an quality supervision bureau inspected Aokai's cables four times and found three batches substandard — and merely fined the company instead of referring the case for prosecution, as required. Inspectors took money and looked away; the construction commission, notified of the problem, simply passed the paper down the chain.

The final bill: 122 officials disciplined in Shaanxi, including 16 at department level and 58 at division level, 17 of them referred for criminal investigation. Aokai was fined 30.5 million yuan, and its legal representative, Wang Zhiwei, was sentenced to life in prison.

The internet gave this episode a nickname: “the layoff that cut an artery.” A man who held the truth about whether an entire metro line's cables met spec could find no functioning channel of correction anywhere along the chain — not in bidding, not in inspection, not in supervision, not in whistleblowing. What finally exposed it was a man who had lost his job and had nothing left to lose.

Young people ride that metro every day. Few stop to ask: what actually protects them — the city's rules, or one sacked employee's conscience? The rules all exist, from the Tendering and Bidding Law to the Product Quality Law, written more completely than anywhere. But on this chain in Xi'an, every rule yielded to connections and money: contracts were won through relationships, inspections were passed through payoffs, silence was kept through complicity. This was not a few bad apples. One hundred and twenty-two disciplined officials tell you it was the system running normally — it just happened, this once, to be exposed.

The hundred-billion-yuan mining case: a signed contract, fourteen years of litigation

The third case is the most instructive of all, because it tests the most basic thing there is: a contract.

In 2003, the Xi'an Institute of Geological and Mineral Exploration — Xikanyuan, a state-owned public institution — signed a Cooperative Exploration Contract with Kechley (Kaijilai) Energy, a private company from Yulin: the institute held the exploration rights, Kechley put up the money — 12 million yuan — to jointly explore the Boluo coalfield in Hengshan County, and any discovery would be shared as agreed. It was the most ordinary arrangement in a market economy: one side has the resource, the other has the capital, all in black and white, signed and sealed.

Then the exploration results came in: 339 square kilometers, geological reserves of 1.568 billion tonnes, a value counted in the hundreds of billions of yuan.

And Xikanyuan stopped honoring the deal. The excuses were many — the contract was never filed, it violated the spirit of a provincial government meeting, the partner company hadn't been incorporated yet when it signed. Meanwhile, the exploration rights were transferred to a third party. Kechley's owner, Zhao Faqi, went to court, and stayed there for over a decade. He won at first instance in the Shaanxi High Court. In 2008, the General Office of the Shaanxi provincial government sent an official letter straight to the Supreme People's Court declaring the contract “invalid.” The Supreme Court remanded; the Shaanxi High Court reversed itself and voided the contract. Zhao appealed and waited another six and a half years, until December 2017, when the Supreme People's Court finally ruled: the contract is valid, and Xikanyuan is in breach.

Think that was the end? It wasn't. The aftermath produced another scandal: in late 2018, the second-instance case file from the Supreme People's Court itself was revealed to have vanished — the surveillance footage, too — until a joint investigation team led by the Central Political and Legal Affairs Commission had to step in. And what did those years do to Zhao Faqi? He was placed on a wanted list. He was jailed. Then he was released without guilt. A man who signed a contract, paid his money, and won his case spent half a lifetime to win back a judgment saying “the contract is valid” and a little over ten million yuan in damages — while the exploration rights to a hundred-billion-yuan coalfield never really returned to the track the contract laid down.

Read this case to the end and you understand the line between a society of connections and a society of contracts. In a contract society, a signature binds, breach costs, and lawsuits are a remedy for the few. Here, a signature is merely the opening of negotiations: when your counterparty is a state institution, the cost of breaking its word is close to zero, while you — a private businessman asking for what you are owed — must first survive the official letters, the connections, the decade of litigation, and ideally the threat of a cell. The rules exist here, too. They simply queue behind power, and take the stage only after power is finished with them.

Three cases, one operating system

Three cases — one about a person, one about a project, one about a contract — running on the same operating system.

Half of its name is bureaucratism: everything runs on rank, on establishment quotas, on organizational procedure. Expertise obeys administration; the market obeys power; when something goes wrong, the first instinct is not correction but cover-up, and when the cover fails, out come the official documents, the procedures, the delays. The other half is the cult of connections: resources are not allocated by a public price list but through networks — who knows whom, who belongs to whom, who can get a word in — and whoever can do that can walk around the rules.

A modern city's logic is the exact opposite. Talent is priced by the market, so the Zhang Xiaopings of the world don't have to resign to prove their worth. Engineering is backstopped by rules and third-party supervision, so safety never depends on one employee's conscience. Contracts are enforced by law, so no signer has to first ask whether the other side is a state institution with people above it. Strangers cooperate through rules, contracts, and law; trust becomes cheap; and the young — who own nothing — are finally qualified to play.

Xi'an's problem is not a shortage of rules, of talent, or of money. It is that its rules rank too low: below rank, below connections, below a leader's face.

Why the young have to leave

Finally, bring it back to the young.

A young person's entire capital is two things: ability, and trust in the rules. He has no connections, no money, no fallback. He can only count on one promise — that this society will price him by his ability, settle with him by contract, and protect him by rules.

Xi'an's three cases smash those three hopes one by one. The Zhang Xiaoping case tells him his ability is priced by rank, not by the market — and the better he is, the more likely the paperwork will brand him a traitor. The cable case tells him every checkpoint of the rules has its price, and his safety is whatever is left over after the bribes. The mining case tells him that even with a signed contract and a won lawsuit, he should be ready to pay for it with fourteen years and his freedom.

So stop asking why Xi'an's young people leave. They are not betraying the ancient capital of thirteen dynasties. They simply read their city's three cases carefully, and voted with their feet. A city that cannot keep its Zhang Xiaopings, cannot protect its Zhao Faqis, and cannot keep its metro riders safe will keep only those who are already settled inside the system — and skilled at turning rules into favors.

Such a place is not for the young. That is not an emotion. It is the joint verdict of three cases.
